claims.title: Depletion and belief claims depend on the exact test
claims.statement: Selected preregistered multilaboratory projects produced small, protocol- and endpoint-dependent depletion estimates; selected measured-belief tests did not establish a reliable protective effect of nonlimited-willpower beliefs.

claims.confidenceRationale: Large projects inform narrow protocol-specific effects, but estimates, endpoints, exclusions and belief designs differ. Nonsignificant results do not establish absence or equivalence.
limitations: Vohs et al. tested 3,531 people across 36 laboratories; overall confirmatory endpoint N=2,461 gave d=.06 (95% CI −.02 to .14). A significant exploratory full-sample d=.08 was a different analysis.

Dang et al. analyzed 1,775 participants across 12 laboratories: primary error-rate d=.10 (95% CI .01 to .19). After auxiliary exclusions that primary estimate stayed .10; only the secondary reaction-time estimate increased to .16.

Hagger et al. reported 2,141 main-analysis participants across 23 laboratories; primary reaction-time variability d=.04 (95% CI −.07 to .15). Accuracy-inclusive analysis also retained a nonsignificant primary estimate while a secondary mean-reaction-time estimate was positive.
Job et al. measured beliefs in Study 1, induced beliefs in Studies 2/3 and used observational self-reports in Study 4. These are distinct designs, not one pooled test.

Carruth et al. analyzed 187 of 194 randomized participants and did not detect the original measured-belief moderation in its modified procedure. Task protocols and exclusions differ; report counts are not a certainty grade, and selected results do not uniquely identify a depleted-resource mechanism.

claims.title: Imagery and confidence in near-threshold reality judgments
claims.statement: In selected near-threshold visual tasks, imagery influenced judgments that a stimulus was externally present; trial-level confidence did not reliably reveal awareness of that influence, although post-task questions showed some global insight.
claims.takeaway: Confidence and vividness are not direct tests of external truth, and a confidence shift alone does not identify its mechanism.
claims.scope: Near-threshold grating-detection and imagery experiments; a separate bias-manipulation report supplies a mechanism boundary, not a direct imagery replication.
claims.confidenceRationale: The reports inform constrained task judgments and local/global insight. Model assumptions, sample-flow discrepancies and selected access limit broader conclusions.
limitations: Dijkstra and Fleming used one critical near-threshold judgment per person and compared specified models. Reused imaging data and nonpreregistered model/imaging analyses do not prove one unique neural mechanism.

The 2023 report gives 272 analyzed in Methods but 274 in Figure 2; Experiment 2 lists exclusion counts that do not reconcile simply with 461 collected and 339 analyzed. These discrepancies remain unresolved.

The 2024 report analyzed 102 and 111 participants, but the post-task global-insight question had 51 and 111 responses. Its plan changed after initial data, and selected Experiment 2 subset/statistic labels remain unresolved.
Local confidence criteria and post-task global insight are different outcomes; this is not evidence that all self-knowledge is absent.

Experiment 2 alone provided inconclusive evidence for no reproduction effect of the base-rate/payoff manipulations; combined evidence was stronger. Benchmark assumptions and unresolved exclusion arithmetic limit interpretation; this was not a direct imagery replication.

Near-threshold grating judgments are not universal tests of perception, autobiographical memory, emotional truth or clinical reality testing, and do not establish that imagined practice equals external competence.
implications: Distinguish what was experienced, what was externally measured and which mechanism the experiment actually discriminated.
notImplied: No claim that imagination and perception are identical or that a vivid feeling makes a belief true.

A separate confidence-manipulation report is not a direct replication or refutation of the imagery experiments.

claims.title: Preschool waiting and later outcomes: qualified associations
claims.statement: Across four selected longitudinal reports, associations between preschool waiting and later outcomes differed by task condition, outcome and analysis; these associations do not establish that training longer waiting improves later life.
claims.takeaway: A waiting-task association is not a forecast of a child’s destiny or a demonstrated benefit from practicing longer waiting.
claims.scope: One Stanford preschool-to-adolescent report and three analyses of the shared NICHD SECCYD cohort through adolescence or age 26. This card concerns long-term associations, not immediate waiting manipulations or a comprehensive intervention review.
claims.confidenceRationale: The reports support bounded descriptions of their own associations, with selective follow-up, varying models and outcomes, shared-cohort dependence and incomplete access to one report. Confidence does not extend to universal prediction or training efficacy.
limitations: Shoda, Mischel and Peake reported condition-specific adolescent associations: 185 returned at least one assessment, 94 had parent-reported SAT scores, and the exposed-reward/no-suggested-strategy SAT subgroup had 35. That subgroup had verbal r=.42 and quantitative r=.57; selective follow-up and a university-community sample limit generalization.

Watts, Duncan and Quan analyzed 918 participants, including a focal maternal-no-college subgroup of 552 and a maternal-college subgroup of 366. In the focal subgroup, standardized age-15 achievement associations were .24 unadjusted, .08 with earlier/background controls and .05 with concurrent controls (p=.140 for the last). Behavioral-composite associations were not statistically significant. Covariate adjustment changes the conditional question, not just the size of one universal effect.

Michaelson and Munakata reported associations for three of five outcomes and problem-behavior associations across models in the same cohort, using different measurements and analyses. Only the abstract and selected indexed primary passages were inspected; detailed Methods, estimates and analysis-specific sample sizes remain unverified here. This is not an independent replication or established causal social-support mechanism.

Sperber and colleagues analyzed 702 participants with a valid preschool task and at least one age-26 outcome. Fully adjusted continuous-delay analyses did not detect statistically significant associations across nine adult outcomes. An exploratory, nonpreregistered full-seven-minute indicator retained a BMI association without multiplicity adjustment. Other categorical specifications yielded different patterns; this is not an only-BMI or all-specifications-null result. Nondetection is not equivalence, and selected Table 1 denominators remain unreconciled.

Observed waiting-to-later-outcome associations do not establish that training longer waiting improves later life. Random assignment of original task conditions does not randomize individual waiting times. This design boundary is not proof that all possible training benefits are absent.

The three SECCYD reports reuse one cohort with different subsets, measures, outcomes and analyses; they are not independent replication votes and their sample sizes must not be added. The four selected reports represent two cohort families, not four independent samples.

Follow-up selection, task ceilings, population differences, outcome measurement and modeling choices constrain comparison. No pooled effect, definitive causal adjustment model, systematic field review, formal risk-of-bias assessment or GRADE certainty rating is supplied.
implications: Name the task, outcome, analysis and cohort before comparing reports. Keep association, prediction and intervention effects distinct.
notImplied: No individual life-success forecast, child ranking, diagnosis, parent blame or judgment of a child’s worth.
No home testing, food restriction, deprivation, deception or clinical recommendation. Waiting longer is not universally better regardless of context or chosen goals.
No proof that waiting predicts nothing, that only BMI can be associated, or that every adjusted categorical analysis is null.
No validation of the site’s integrated self-command method and no claim that possible training benefits are absent throughout the literature.

claims.title: Brain training: practiced gains are not the same as broad transfer
claims.statement: In these selected cognitive-training reports, gains on practiced or closely related tasks did not consistently extend to distinct cognitive tests; the results did not establish broad everyday or clinical benefits.
claims.takeaway: Getting better at a brain-training game does not by itself show that the gain carries over. Ask what was tested, compared with what, and how long after practice.
claims.scope: Three nonclinical training experiments and one working-memory synthesis spanning unselected samples and cognitive or learning difficulties. This is a bounded report comparison, not a comprehensive review of cognitive enhancement, rehabilitation or dementia prevention.
claims.confidenceRationale: The reports support task- and comparator-specific observations, including some positive untrained-test effects. Attrition, allocation differences, small samples, mixed synthesis populations, overlapping study families and limited follow-up constrain broader conclusions.
limitations: Owen and colleagues analyzed 11,430 of 52,617 registrants after six weeks, with greater control dropout. Practiced tasks improved; small positive reasoning differences versus active knowledge-question control (d=.17 and .22) coexist with differing memory results. The article’s intention-to-treat label does not mean all registrants were analyzed, and the six-week endpoint is not delayed retention.

Jaeggi and colleagues analyzed 34 training and 35 no-training control participants across four matched cohorts. A positive speeded matrix-test interaction was measured 1–2 days after training. No original active control or participant-randomization method was reported; tests differed across cohorts, so neither standardized IQ-point gains nor randomized dose-response conclusions follow.

Redick and colleagues analyzed 73 cognitive-test completers after substantial attrition and mixed allocation procedures. Practiced-task gains were not accompanied by statistically significant positive cognitive transfer at the article-stated α=.01 threshold. Small effects are not excluded. Reported daily-activity changes were not behaviorally verified, and delayed retention was not assessed.

The mixed-population synthesis reported treated-control nonverbal-ability g=.05 (95% CI −.02 to .13), alongside positive related-task estimates. Raw positive reading-comprehension (g=.15) and delayed-arithmetic (g=.22) estimates were reduced in author sensitivity analyses (.08 and .14); positive subgroups also existed. It is inaccurate to describe every estimate as zero or nonsignificant. Sparse, varied follow-up does not establish healthy-only durable benefit.

Practiced tasks, structurally related tasks, distinct cognitive tests, self-reported daily changes and observed everyday functioning are different outcomes. Assessment immediately after training differs from later retention. These reports do not establish general everyday competence, dementia prevention or targeted clinical rehabilitation efficacy.

The synthesis includes Jaeggi and Redick study families but excludes Owen under its outcome criteria. Its Jaeggi-labelled comparisons include author-supplied data absent from the original article; those do not turn the original experiment into an active-controlled study. Shared controls and included trials prevent counting comparisons or reports as independent confirmation votes.

This bounded selection is not a systematic field review, formal certainty assessment or raw-data reanalysis. Nondetection is not proof of zero effect, and none of these findings validates the site’s integrated learning method.

No brain-mechanism equivalence, universal talent increase, commercial-product guarantee or validation of a custom self-command method.

claims.title: Gratitude writing: comparator and follow-up matter
claims.statement: The selected gratitude-writing experiment found a reported wellbeing difference against specific comparison tasks, while a broader synthesis found comparator-dependent estimates. These findings do not establish a universal or reliably lasting benefit from gratitude writing.
claims.takeaway: Ask what the gratitude activity was compared with, which outcome changed, and when it was measured—not just whether a result was positive.
claims.scope: One nonclinical undergraduate writing experiment and one historical synthesis spanning different ages, activities and wellbeing measures. This is a bounded report comparison, not an adult-only pooled estimate or a comprehensive review of gratitude, health or treatment.
claims.confidenceRationale: The inspected reports distinguish some positive comparator-specific findings from nondetections and sensitivity analyses. Completer selection, unknown initial allocation/attrition, unreported exact ages, mixed synthesis populations, comparator assumptions and limited follow-up constrain generalization.
limitations: Watkins and colleagues analyzed 129 completers/adherers: 47 gratitude, 42 comparative pride and 40 semantic memory. Baseline-adjusted composite wellbeing favored gratitude across post-activity assessments. The composite does not establish each component separately; initial randomized numbers, arm-specific attrition and exact ages remain unknown.

The writing experiment’s time-by-condition interaction was not statistically significant. Separate occasion analyses found a statistically significant overall condition effect only five weeks after the activity; the immediate and one-week tests were not statistically significant. Descriptive continued improvement is not a demonstrated differential growth trajectory, and nondetection is not proof of zero differences.

The controls were specific: semantic autobiographical description and positive-event processing emphasizing superiority to others. They do not represent all memory writing, pride or positive activities. All groups were told the activity intended to improve happiness; equal expectancy was not established. The one-week study schedule is descriptive, not an optimal-dose recommendation.

The historical synthesis reported a small wellbeing difference versus activity-matched tasks (d=.14, 95% CI .01 to .27) and no statistically significant difference versus psychologically active alternatives (d=−.03, −.13 to .07). Its mixed populations, formats and measures are not a pooled answer for adult gratitude writing alone; nondetection does not establish equivalence.

The activity-matched estimate no longer excluded zero in the synthesis authors’ trim-and-fill sensitivity. This is method-dependent sensitivity, not a corrected true effect or proof that gratitude activities are ineffective. The synthesis does not provide a separately established long-term persistence estimate.

Follow-ups within the writing experiment are not separate replications. The synthesis’s comparator and outcome subsets overlap and cannot be added as independent confirmations. The listed 2015 experiment was not found in its inspected inclusion material; an included Watkins 2008 report is different, and participant-level independence has not been certified.

This bounded review is not a systematic field review, formal certainty assessment or raw-data reanalysis. It does not establish an optimal practice, a causal cognitive mechanism or the efficacy of the site’s integrated method.

claims.title: Helping, liking and romantic attraction are different outcomes.
claims.statement: A low-cost puzzle experiment found greater immediate liking after a friendly personal request than after experimenter-instructed help. Separate request-compliance studies examined anticipated refusal discomfort and task responses. These findings do not establish that giving favors creates romantic attraction or durable attachment.
claims.takeaway: Keep helping behavior, immediate liking and romantic interest separate; agreeing to a request does not by itself establish romantic interest.
claims.scope: One undergraduate puzzle experiment in Japan and the US, plus selected Studies 5–6 from a separate compliance report. Both puzzle groups helped. This is a bounded outcome-and-design comparison, not a comprehensive review of relationships or a dating strategy.
claims.confidenceRationale: The original liking comparison is narrow and immediate; the friendly-request package changes several features together. Small convenience samples, self-report measures, hypothetical compliance judgments, complete-case selection and request-logistics differences constrain generalization. Romantic desire and durable attachment were not tested in the inspected experiment and selected compliance studies.
limitations: Niiya reported 83 undergraduates: Japan 22 personal-request and 19 experimenter-instruction, US 22 and 20. Immediate liking change was greater in the personal-request condition. The liking measure combined liking and friendship-oriented items; it was not a romantic-desire measure.

Both puzzle groups helped the same confederate. The personal request included praise and a question, while the comparator was an experimenter’s instruction. Requester identity, authority and wording changed together; the result does not isolate doing a favor itself or establish communicated closeness as the causal mechanism.

The puzzle study’s nonsignificant comparator liking changes do not establish zero change or a necessary direct-request condition. A nonsignificant country interaction is not equivalence. In the US instruction condition, perceived closeness did increase significantly even though liking did not; the outcomes must not be collapsed.

The puzzle samples were predominantly women, and all confederates were women from the corresponding social group. Ratings followed the brief task. The inspected experiment does not establish effects for costly or pressured requests, ongoing relationships, months of one-way giving, romantic desire or durable attachment.

Flynn and Lake’s Study 5 reports 83 completers making hypothetical judgments. A separate vignette sample rated anticipated refusal discomfort higher for direct requests; its sample size was not established here. These are not reports of actual field recipients’ motives. Help-seekers’ higher indirect-request estimate was not statistically significant, and neither measure establishes affection.

Flynn and Lake’s Study 6 analyzed 79 of 99 initial participants after 16 withdrawals and 4 incomplete cases. Direct verbal requests and silently handed-out flyers also differed in contact and return logistics. Nonreturns were assigned a capped value in the flyer outcome; exact cell allocation remains unreconciled. This is a task-compliance comparison, not an isolated pressure mechanism or an attraction test.

Niiya’s online 2015 and issue 2016 versions are one report, with two country samples under a shared protocol. Flynn and Lake’s selected studies and separate manipulation-check sample belong to a different report. Different outcomes, samples and report versions must not be pooled into a participant total or counted as independent confirmations of a favor-causes-liking claim.

This bounded review is not a systematic field review, formal certainty assessment, raw-data reanalysis or validation of a custom method. No official correction or retraction was identified in the limited checks; report integrity remains unknown. Independent human scientific review is pending.
implications: Ask which response was actually measured, against which comparator and at what time. Preserve a person’s freedom to decline.

claims.title: Familiar is not the same as true
claims.statement: In experiments with factual statements, prior exposure can raise later truth judgments—including judgments of false statements. That is a change in judgment, not new evidence for the claim. Knowing relevant facts helps, but does not always prevent this effect. Initial accuracy-focused evaluation can reduce susceptibility under some tested conditions; it is not a universal safeguard.
claims.takeaway: Before treating a familiar claim as established, ask: “What evidence supports it, and are these sources genuinely independent?” Separate what you remember hearing from what has been checked. When you have relevant knowledge, compare the claim with it; when you do not, mark the uncertainty and check a reliable source.
claims.scope: Selected experiments on repetition and judgments of complete factual statements; not an exhaustive synthesis or a perceptual-confidence finding.
claims.confidenceRationale: The narrow repeated/new truth-judgment contrast is supported across the selected reports. Task-dependent knowledge and initial-evaluation boundaries, shared investigative programs and limited populations constrain generalization; this editorial label is not a formal certainty grade.
limitations: Initial accuracy-focused evaluation is a tested boundary, not a universal safeguard. Brashier et al. Experiment 2’s task×knowledge×repetition interaction was not significant (p=.133); Experiments 3 and 4 provided direct interaction tests. Nonsignificant simple effects do not establish equivalence. Initial truth evaluation is not external source verification.

This is propositional truth judgment about factual statements, not perceptual confidence, self-efficacy, objective truth or demonstrated competence. Scale-point increases are not percentage increases in belief; binary item-judgment proportions are not percentages of people who permanently believe a claim.

Three original reports cover seven principal reported experiments/cohorts: two Fazio, four Brashier and one Henderson longitudinal cohort. Individual participant identities were not deduplicated. Fazio and Brashier share authors/lab; four test phases within Henderson are not four independent replications. No pooled unique participant total is justified.

Purposive audit, not an exhaustive or systematic review. Small selected samples, narrow trivia, post-exposure knowledge checks, attrition and exclusions limit transfer. Publication bias was not estimated; data/code were not rerun; no formal certainty grading or human-expert approval is claimed.

The suggested source-checking prompt is a cautious epistemic practice, not a validated intervention or promise of immunity. Its full sequence, external checking step, durable benefit and wellbeing effect were not tested by these reports. This evidence does not justify discouraging repetition of verified material as a learning method; accurate retention is a different question.
implications: Separate what you remember hearing from what has been checked. The suggested prompt is not a study-tested program.
notImplied: Repetition does not establish factual truth, durable worldview change, behavior, learning benefit or wellbeing.
No uniquely demonstrated cognitive-ease or familiarity mechanism. Repetition changes multiple memory/process cues; model fit does not isolate a unique mediator.
Knowledge is useful but not an automatic shield. These findings do not mean facts are useless, thinking makes no difference or affirmations change reality.
questions: How do these effects and accuracy-evaluation boundaries generalize beyond selected trivia tasks and populations?

claims.title: Restricted sleep opportunity can impair sustained attention
claims.statement: In two selected controlled laboratory studies of healthy adults, repeated restriction of sleep opportunity worsened some measures of sustained attention compared with longer sleep opportunities. The pattern depended on the schedule and the measure used.
claims.takeaway: When evaluating a sleep-and-performance claim, ask which sleep schedule was compared and which attention measure changed. A laboratory group result does not determine an individual's safe sleep duration or fitness to drive.
claims.scope: Selected repeated partial-restriction results from Belenky (2003) and Lo (2012), measured with psychomotor-vigilance tasks. Not a review of total sleep deprivation, clinical sleep disorders, memory consolidation or all cognitive abilities.
claims.confidenceRationale: Controlled schedule comparisons support a narrow attention finding, but selected samples, endpoint-specific missingness, different outcomes and uncertain allocation details in one report limit generalization. This is a bounded review, not a systematic synthesis or formal certainty grade.
limitations: Belenky enrolled 66 healthy commercial-license holders; technical losses left 56 participants with usable vigilance data. Randomization was not established in the inspected methods. Some performance patterns plateaued and not all schedule comparisons differed.

Lo used a counterbalanced crossover: 36 entrants and three withdrawals, not two independent samples or 36 complete pairs. One habituation night and one baseline night preceded the experimental schedules. The slowest-decile result was response speed normalized to baseline, not percentage attention lost.

Belenky reused data from the Balkin 2000 DOT report; those publications are one study family. Lo's crossover periods and repeated tests are not independent replications. No pooled participant total or common effect size is claimed.

Time in bed is an opportunity for sleep, not identical to measured sleep. Laboratory schedules also change time awake and other contextual factors; these results do not isolate a biological mechanism. Small selected samples and different endpoints limit transfer to other populations and everyday tasks.

This two-report synthesis excludes Van Dongen (2003) while the content and impact of its indexed 2004 erratum remain unresolved. Exclusion is not a finding that its results are false or retracted. No comprehensive correction audit, raw-data reanalysis, systematic search or human scientific acceptance is claimed.
implications: Keep the exposure, comparator, measured outcome and population visible before generalizing.
notImplied: No personal sleep-hours prescription, fitness-to-drive assessment, or encouragement to restrict sleep or push through fatigue.
No universal daily decline, percentage loss of attention, or conclusion that people invariably fail to feel sleepier.
No validation of the transcript's broader memory, reasoning or biological-mechanism claims, or of a Sovereign Psychology method.

claims.title: Feeling more excited does not guarantee better performance
claims.statement: Brief excitement instructions have shown benefits in some laboratory performance tasks, but findings are mixed: a later direct speech replication found no improvement in observer-rated performance, and a different math-task study found no performance benefit.
claims.takeaway: Feeling more excited, feeling less anxious and performing better are separate outcomes. A useful-feeling reframe is not by itself evidence of improved performance or a biological explanation.
claims.scope: Selected immediate student laboratory outcomes in Brooks (2014), Poynter and Pasqualini (2025), and Ganley and colleagues (2021). Not an exhaustive review, clinical treatment evaluation or test of durable change.
claims.confidenceRationale: Original positive findings are bounded by later nonreplication and a different-task null result. Differences in instructions, comparisons, measurement and sampling prevent a general efficacy conclusion. This editorial label is not a formal certainty grade.
limitations: Brooks reported different instructions and comparisons across singing, speech and math tasks. The math instruction was displayed rather than the same spoken self-statement used in other tasks. Positive results belong to the particular comparisons, not a universal phrase.

Poynter and Pasqualini directly replicated and extended the speech task: higher reported excitement did not translate into improved observer ratings. Early stopping and changes from planned two-tailed to one-tailed tests limit certainty; no significant benefit is not proof of equivalence. Speech duration was not analyzed.

Ganley and colleagues used a different math task and comparator context, making this a conceptual test rather than an exact replication. Its performance null and inconclusive excitement-induction check do not establish that the strategy can never help.

The original report contains multiple tasks within one research program; these are not independent-laboratory replications. The later speech and math reports use separate recruitment and different outcomes. No pooled effect or unique participant total is claimed.

Retrospective feeling ratings, selected student samples, exclusions, missing observer data and varied task incentives limit transfer. Registration contents and participant-level data were not independently reanalyzed; no comprehensive correction audit or systematic synthesis is claimed. Independent human scientific review is pending.

Measured appraisal associations do not establish a causal mechanism, and limited heart-rate comparisons do not establish identical bodily responses to anxiety and excitement. Changes in reported excitement, anxiety and performance must remain separate.
implications: Compare the instruction, comparator, measured feeling and task outcome before judging a performance claim. A personally useful experience can be recorded without treating it as proof of general efficacy.
notImplied: No treatment claim for anxiety disorders, guaranteed real-world gains, lasting change, or validation of a Sovereign Psychology method.
No requirement to deny anxiety, force a belief, or conclude that difficulty reflects insufficient willpower.
Related appraisal and regulation-choice claims address different questions; they do not confirm these excitement instructions.
questions: Which instructions, task conditions and populations reliably benefit, if any, and do results extend beyond immediate laboratory outcomes?
claims.population: Selected student samples in singing, speech and mathematics tasks; not clinical efficacy samples.
claims.reviewer: AI-assisted scoped research and independent AI critique; independent human scientific review pending

history.change: Added a mixed-evidence excitement/performance dossier after independent AI critique, distinguishing original results, direct speech replication and conceptual math testing. No exercise or efficacy promise added.

claims.title: Self-rated assertiveness is not demonstrated behavior
claims.statement: In one adult trial, an eight-week online CBT package improved self-rated assertiveness relative to a wait-list at the end of treatment. This does not establish that a brief communication script improves everyday relationships.
claims.takeaway: Separate how assertive someone reports feeling from observed behavior and real-world outcomes. A personally useful conversation does not establish the effectiveness of a training package, and a package result does not validate every communication tip.
claims.scope: Hagberg and colleagues (2023), an eight-week adult online multicomponent CBT trial and its self-report endpoints. Not an exhaustive review or evaluation of a short script.
claims.confidenceRationale: One selected trial with self-report endpoints, substantial differential missingness and a wait-list comparison supports only a bounded package-level conclusion. This editorial label is not a formal certainty grade.
limitations: The trial randomized 210 adults and excluded five after randomization for concurrent therapy, leaving 205 analyzed: 67 unguided, 70 guided and 68 wait-list participants.

Week-eight measurements were available for 35/67 unguided, 50/70 guided and 61/68 wait-list participants; year-one measurements for 30/67 and 38/70 active-arm participants. These are measurement-completion counts, not model sample sizes. Substantial differential missingness remains a limitation despite mixed-model and imputation handling.
One-year active-group outcomes were compared with the wait-list’s week-eight outcomes, not a concurrent untreated one-year group. This does not establish controlled one-year efficacy.

The package combined multiple CBT components and measured self-rated assertiveness. It did not isolate a brief script or establish observed assertive behavior, better everyday relationships, or a causal mechanism.

A nonsignificant guided-versus-unguided contrast is not proof of equivalence. The RAS measure changed from secondary to primary after registration; the timing of that change was not independently audited. Participant-level data were not reanalyzed. Independent human scientific review is pending.
implications: Check what was actually practiced, measured and compared before transferring a training result to a communication tip.
notImplied: No relationship cure, guarantee of safe confrontation, clinical advice, or validation of a Sovereign Psychology method.
No requirement to confront someone or explain a boundary. No exercise or short-script efficacy claim follows from this trial.
The related expression question is not additional supporting evidence for this training package.
questions: Do improvements extend to observed behavior and everyday relationships, and which package components contribute?
claims.population: Adults recruited for an online assertiveness-training trial; results do not establish effectiveness in every relationship or setting.
claims.reviewer: AI-assisted scoped research and independent AI critique; independent human scientific review pending
