Failure is not a clean demonstration that prediction error or reconsolidation never matters. Kindt declares clinic co-founder interest.
sources.design: Preregistered same-laboratory replication of Sevenster2014; altered stimuli/instructions; no/single/multiple prediction-error conditions, all propranolol.
sources.population: Final analyzed sample: 91 university students aged 18–35; groups 30/31/30. Total recruited not independently extracted.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 91 final analyzed; recruitment total not independently extracted

sources.title: Social isolation, loneliness, and all-cause mortality in older men and women
sources.accessDepth: Selected live full-text introduction, Results, Tables 2–3 and measurement definition in institutional-hosted journal PDF, pp.5797–5800; not a complete methods/supplement audit.
sources.summary: Objective contact/participation and subjective loneliness were distinct measures, weakly correlated in this older-adult cohort. Mortality associations varied with construct and adjustment. Observational results do not establish causation, individual prognosis, or that loneliness is harmless.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 6,500 participants; not an intervention trial
sources.design: 2004–05 isolation/contact and UCLA loneliness measures; mortality follow-up averaged 7.25 years.
sources.population: 6,500 English Longitudinal Study of Ageing participants aged 52+; 918 deaths.

sources.title: Acute social isolation evokes midbrain craving responses similar to hunger
sources.accessDepth: Selected live full-text abstract/results, Methods Participants/design and reporting-summary recruitment; linked publisher correction read.
sources.summary: After 10 hours of experimental isolation, normally connected healthy adults reported increased social craving. Selected cue-evoked brain responses were examined separately. This acute deprivation study is not a model of every experience alone, chronic loneliness, or treatment efficacy.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 42 recruited; 40 complete datasets
sources.design: Counterbalanced baseline, 10-hour fasting and 10-hour isolation conditions with self-report and cue-evoked fMRI.
sources.population: 42 recruited; 40 complete datasets, ages 18–40; 27 women.
sources.correctionNote: 2022 author correction changes Figure 5 caption abbreviations/order for putamen and caudate. It is attached to this report, not counted as independent evidence.

sources.title: Daily Well-Being: The Role of Autonomy, Competence, and Relatedness
sources.accessDepth: Selected original-article Methods p.422 in public full-text rendering explicitly attributed to coauthor Shelly L. Gable; independent AI reviewer also checked Limitations p.432. Prior publisher abstract and institutional indexed Results p.425 retained. No complete-document or raw-data audit; direct institutional PDF remained inaccessible.
sources.summary: Daily autonomy, competence and relatedness showed distinct associations with well-being in a 14-day student diary study. Association does not show that autonomy or competence replaces relatedness or that any custom framework cures loneliness.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 76 students; 9 incomplete; 67 analyzed
sources.design: Fourteen nightly paper diaries of need satisfaction and well-being; person-level and within-person observational associations.
sources.population: 76 introductory-psychology students; 9 incomplete, leaving 67 analyzed (29 men, 38 women), ages 17–68; 86% under 26.

sources.title: Solitude as an Approach to Affective Self-Regulation
sources.accessDepth: Selected live full-text methods/results for Studies 1–4, General Discussion and Limitations; not every analysis rechecked.
sources.summary: Brief solitude generally lowered positive and negative high-arousal affect. Low-arousal composite results varied; these were not loneliness-treatment endpoints. Experienced autonomy in Study 4 was measured, not randomly assigned. No universal benefit, durable cure or personal solitude dose follows.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Separate studies: 114, 108 and 343; Study 4 recruited 173 and analyzed 157. No pooled sample claimed.
sources.design: Undergraduate experiments using 15-minute solitude; Study 4 two-week switching-replications diary design.
sources.population: Separate undergraduate studies: 114, 108 and 343 participants; Study 4 recruited 173 and analyzed 157. Some arm/allocation totals remain unreconciled; not a pooled sample.

sources.title: Effect of Layperson-Delivered, Empathy-Focused Program of Telephone Calls on Loneliness, Depression, and Anxiety Among Adults During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Randomized Clinical Trial
sources.accessDepth: Selected live full-text Methods, outcomes, discussion and limitations.
sources.summary: Four weeks of empathy-focused calls improved UCLA loneliness versus no-call control. The De Jong difference was not statistically significant; no statistically significant between-group change was detected on the social-network measure. No active attention control separated empathy from receiving calls, and durability was not established.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 240 randomized, 120 per arm; 13 intervention and 1 control lost to follow-up
sources.design: Four weeks of empathy-focused telephone calls versus no-call control; blinded outcome assessor.
sources.population: 240 Meals on Wheels clients, 120 per arm; ages 27–101; 63% aged 65 or older; 13 intervention versus 1 control lost to follow-up.

sources.title: Internet-Based Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Loneliness: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.accessDepth: Selected live author-accepted full-text abstract, methods/results and limitations; not all supplementary material.
sources.summary: Eight-week guided internet CBT reduced loneliness relative to waitlist in a small pilot. No active comparator isolated therapist contact; differential missingness and a missing-at-random assumption matter. The original trial does not establish durability, specific mechanism or clear clinical importance.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 73 randomized; 61 post-assessments for loneliness (27 intervention, 34 waitlist)
sources.design: Eight-week guided internet CBT; intention-to-treat analysis under missing-at-random assumption.
sources.population: 98 assessed; 73 randomized (36 guided ICBT, 37 waitlist); 61 post-assessments for the loneliness outcome (27/34).

sources.title: The effectiveness of psychological interventions for loneliness: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.accessDepth: Author institutional abstract and PubMed abstract, plus selected search-indexed primary accepted-manuscript inclusion row for Käll et al. (2020), p.24. Live accepted PDF link errored and direct institutional request returned HTTP403; full risk-of-bias/overlap tables not audited.
sources.summary: The review reported a small-to-medium pooled reduction in loneliness across varied psychological interventions, with heterogeneity and mixed study quality. Its inclusion of the Käll pilot is confirmed, so the review is not an independent replication of that trial. Detailed bias tables remain unaudited.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 31 RCTs / 3,959 participants reviewed; 28 RCTs / 3,039 participants meta-analyzed. These are overlapping report totals, not one recruited cohort.
sources.design: Five-database review; psychological interventions across populations and delivery methods.
sources.population: 31 RCTs / 3,959 participants reviewed; 28 RCTs / 3,039 meta-analyzed.

sources.title: Modulation of muscle responses evoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation during the acquisition of new fine motor skills
sources.accessDepth: Selected original full-text methods, results and discussion in public upload explicitly attributed to coauthor Joaquim Brasil-Neto; publisher returned 403.
sources.summary: In the small imagery experiment, mental and physical piano practice produced similar TMS-map changes but different behavioral gains. Similarity was not formal equivalence; the imagery group also had physical tests. Neither identical neural firing nor structural permanence was established.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Experiment 1: 18 (6 per group). Imagery Experiment 2: 15 (5 per group). Separate samples, not a pooled trial.
sources.design: Random group assignment; five days of two-hour mental or physical piano-sequence practice. All groups physically performed daily tests; imagery movements were monitored.
sources.population: Experiment 1: 18, 6/group. Imagery Experiment 2: 15, 5/group, ages 19–42; right-handed instrument/keyboard novices.

sources.title: Does mental practice still enhance performance? A 24 Year follow-up and meta-analytic replication and extension
sources.accessDepth: Publisher abstract/highlights plus selected search-indexed Results/Discussion section snippets; full methods and inclusion table not read.
sources.summary: A publication-bias-adjusted mental-practice estimate was small (r=.131). The authors treated multiple effects as independent and acknowledged potentially inflated significance. The 115 effects are not 115 independent studies or a percentage of physical-practice effectiveness.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 37 studies, 115 effects; participant total not independently extracted and within-study effect dependence was not modeled.
sources.design: Meta-analysis with publication-bias adjustment and moderator analyses, but multiple effects per study treated as independent.
sources.population: 37 studies, 115 effects; multiple effects per article were treated as independent. Participant total not extracted.

sources.title: Visuo-motor learning with combination of different rates of motor imagery and physical practice
sources.accessDepth: Publisher abstract only; paywalled full text not purchased.
sources.summary: The abstract describes task-specific movement-time benefits in an object-grasp/insertion task using different imagery allocations. Percentages describe training-trial allocation, not universal effectiveness. Full sample, allocation, accuracy, equivalence and delayed outcomes were not verified.
sources.design: Object-grasp/insertion task: 240 trials with 0/25/50/75% imagery allocations, plus irrelevant-imagery control.
sources.population: Participant denominator not extracted from accessible abstract.

sources.title: Learning by doing and learning by thinking: an fMRI study of combining motor and mental training
sources.accessDepth: Publisher full text, selected Methods, behavioral/neural Results and Discussion.
sources.summary: Combined mental and physical practice improved an untrained finger sequence in this experiment. The combined group trained longer; a small additional volume control does not decisively remove that confound. Near motor transfer is not evidence of interpersonal transfer or a causal neural mechanism.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 30 randomized, 10 per arm; MRI subset 18; additional physical-volume control 6.
sources.design: Six weeks of finger-sequence training; single-modality groups practiced 72 minutes, combined group 144 minutes. Posttest 1–2 days after the final session.
sources.population: 30 healthy right-handed participants randomized 10/arm; 18 MRI subset. Additional physical-volume control n=6.

sources.title: To What Extent Can Motor Imagery Replace Motor Execution While Learning a Fine Motor Skill?
sources.accessDepth: Search-indexed primary full-text Methods/Results/Discussion; live PMC CAPTCHA prevented direct open. Not an abstract-only reading or a live full-document read.
sources.summary: Greater physical execution favored later response speed; explicit imagery had no detectable advantage over withholding responses. Accuracy differed from speed, and preparation was possible in both groups. Nonsignificance is not equivalence or proof that imagery never helps.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 24 participants; 7 men and 17 women; ages 20–30.
sources.design: Imagery-after-NoGo versus withhold groups; sequences with 0–100% execution over two days, execution test on consecutive third day. Randomization not established in read methods.
sources.population: 24 university students, 7 men and 17 women, ages 20–30; 21 right-handed and 3 left-handed.

sources.title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
sources.accessDepth: Selected full primary methods/results and general discussion in coauthor laboratory PDF, linked from laboratory Projects page.
sources.summary: Restudy favored immediate prose recall, whereas retrieval practice favored delayed recall. Restudy also produced higher predicted remembering despite poorer week-later recall. Tasks were verbal; some study and test periods differed in duration. No motor, interpersonal or identity transfer was tested.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Experiment 1: 120; Experiment 2: 180. Separate experiments, not a pooled trial.
sources.design: Prose learning with restudy or free-recall practice without feedback. Experiment 1 counterbalanced within-person learning conditions; delay between subjects. Experiment 2 used three sequences of four study/test periods, with 30 per sequence-by-delay cell.
sources.population: Experiment 1: 120 Washington University undergraduates; Experiment 2: 180; ages 18–24. Do not represent as one pooled trial.

sources.title: Repeated Testing Produces Superior Transfer of Learning Relative to Repeated Studying
sources.accessDepth: Selected primary full-text methods/results/discussion in public author upload. Page explicitly attributes upload to Andrew C. Butler, 28 June 2016. No reliance on ResearchGate recommendations or comments; supplement not read.
sources.summary: Retrieval with correct-answer feedback improved one-week retention and prompted inference transfer relative to the restudy comparisons. Prompts signaled relevant prior knowledge; spontaneous everyday application was not tested. Recall and application contributions were inseparable, and some comparisons differed in time-on-task.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Experiment 1a: 24; 1b: 24; 2: 24; 3: 20. Some conditional analyses have smaller denominators.
sources.design: Within-person, counterbalanced text materials; repeated cued recall with correct-answer feedback versus restudy. Tests repeated earlier questions or asked new within-domain/cross-domain inference questions.
sources.population: Washington University psychology undergraduates: Experiment 1a n=24; 1b n=24; 2 n=24; 3 n=20. Conditional analyses have smaller denominators.
sources.correctionNote: A later primary article’s Footnote 1 attributes the original Experiment 3 d=.99 to a standard-deviation calculation error and reports d=1.17, citing 2016 correspondence. No formal erratum was located and no independent recalculation performed; do not reuse the original effect unqualified.

sources.title: The Testing Effect and Far Transfer: The Role of Exposure to Key Information
sources.accessDepth: Publisher primary full text: selected methods/results for both experiments, discussion and Footnote 1; raw data not reanalyzed.
sources.summary: Using Butler’s materials, retrieval outperformed rereading; adding isolated key information reduced but did not remove the advantage. This is prompted laboratory transfer, with differing time-on-task. It is neither spontaneous far transfer nor an independent new set of materials.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Experiment 1: 56; Experiment 2: 55 participated, 54 analyzed. Endpoint-specific missing records are separate.
sources.design: Replication/extension of Butler 2010 Experiment 3 using original materials. Retrieval plus feedback versus rereading; second experiment added rereading plus isolated key statements.
sources.population: Erasmus psychology undergraduates: Experiment 1 n=56 (28 per delay); Experiment 2 55 participating, 54 analyzed. Some acquisition/timing records were missing, distinct from final-test sample.

sources.title: The Neural Bases of Distraction and Reappraisal
sources.accessDepth: Selected original Methods and self-report/neural Results in a public coauthor-laboratory-linked PDF; not whole-document reading. Live PMC CAPTCHA and an institutional download rate limit were not bypassed.
sources.summary: Distraction and reappraisal each reduced immediate negative-affect ratings relative to attending naturally. Reappraisal reduced ratings more, whereas distraction reduced amygdala activity more. Neural activity is not interchangeable with felt relief; no delayed clinical-anxiety outcome was tested.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 18 women in main experiment; separate effort pilot 23 and timing pilot 10, not pooled.
sources.design: Within-person negative-picture task, six-letter working-memory distraction, situation reinterpretation, and attend control; counterbalanced stimulus pairing.
sources.population: 18 women from Stanford campus community, mean 24.4; separate effort pilot 23 and timing pilot 10 are not pooled with imaging sample.

sources.title: Emotion-Regulation Choice
sources.accessDepth: Selected full primary methods/results and discussion in author university PDF.
sources.summary: After strategy training, participants more often chose distraction at higher intensity and reappraisal at lower intensity. These are choice patterns, not evidence that their choices optimized longer-term outcomes.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Three separate healthy-student experiments: 20, 20, 16; no pooled trial.
sources.design: Repeated choices after training in distraction/reappraisal; low/high-intensity pictures or calibrated electric stimulation.
sources.population: Three healthy-student experiments: 20, 20, 16; not one pooled trial.

sources.title: The Psychological Health Benefits of Accepting Negative Emotions and Thoughts: Laboratory, Diary, and Longitudinal Evidence
sources.accessDepth: Selected original full Methods, Study 3 Results/Table4, limitations and publisher supplement project-lineage disclosure; not all models or raw data audited. Publisher project-lineage supplement: https://supp.apa.org/psycarticles/supplemental/pspp0000157/pspp0000157_supp.html
sources.summary: Measured nonjudgment of inner experiences was associated with less negative stress reactivity and better psychological-health indicators. Acceptance was not randomly assigned; statistical mediation is not a demonstrated causal mechanism. Study 3 shares a larger Denver project with Troy 2013; exact participant overlap is unresolved.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Study 1: 1003 students across three samples; Study 2: 156 of 160 women; Study 3:222 of 340 enrolled, 247 invited to diaries. Not a pooled cohort.
sources.design: Measured habitual acceptance: cross-sectional, standardized-stressor, and fourteen-day diary/six-month longitudinal studies. Not randomized acceptance training.
sources.population: Study 1 final 459/336/208 students (1003). Study 2 final 156 of 160 women. Study 3 final 222 of 340 enrolled; only 247 invited to diaries (not 118 simple attrition).

sources.title: Hiding Feelings: The Acute Effects of Inhibiting Negative and Positive Emotion
sources.accessDepth: Selected full primary Methods, subjective/behavioral Results and Discussion in coauthor laboratory PDF.
sources.summary: Suppressing visible expression reduced displayed emotion without a detected reduction in reported sadness; amusement and physiological patterns differed. This acute film experiment does not establish equivalence, inevitable rebound, illness or universal harm from restraint.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 180 female students analyzed; two additional participants excluded for equipment failure.
sources.design: Random assignment to suppress visible expressions or watch naturally; all watched counterbalanced amusing, neutral and sad films.
sources.population: 180 female introductory-psychology students analyzed; two additional excluded for equipment failure.

sources.title: The Social Consequences of Expressive Suppression
sources.accessDepth: Selected primary Methods, Results and Discussion for both studies.
sources.summary: In unfamiliar female dyads, assigned expressive suppression reduced responsiveness and increased partners’ blood-pressure responses. Lower rapport and affiliation were statistically clear only in Study 2. Acute self-reported affiliation is not lasting friendship loss; relational and cultural context matter.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Study 1: 72 women/36 dyads; Study 2: 84 women/42 dyads. Separate studies, not a pooled trial.
sources.design: Unacquainted pairs discussed an upsetting film. Dyads and regulating member assigned; suppression versus reappraisal/control in Study 1, suppression versus control in Study 2.
sources.population: Study 1: 72 women, 36 dyads (12/group). Study 2: 84 women, 42 dyads (21/group), Stanford community/undergraduates.

sources.title: Situational Strategies for Self-Control
sources.accessDepth: Selected live PMC author-manuscript sections; not full cited-study audit. Publisher timed out.
sources.summary: Organizes situation selection/modification, attention, cognitive change and response modulation; notes constraints and costs rather than establishing one universally superior strategy. No experimental test of the whole model. A cited Ariely/Wertenbroch 2002 report was retracted in 2026; its findings are not inherited here. Review itself is not thereby retracted.
sources.sampleSizeNote: No new recruited sample.
sources.design: Conceptual process model and narrative review; no new experimental sample or whole-model trial.
sources.population: Not applicable: conceptual/narrative review with no newly recruited participants.

relatedPublications.title: Retraction: Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment
relatedPublications.note: This 2026 notice retracts the cited Ariely and Wertenbroch (2002) report (DOI 10.1111/1467-9280.00441), not this citing report. Its findings are not inherited as evidence here; this host report and its separately described results are not thereby retracted.

sources.title: More Than Resisting Temptation: Beneficial Habits Mediate the Relationship Between Self-Control and Positive Life Outcomes
sources.accessDepth: Direct primary abstract; selected search-indexed original Methods for Studies 1, 3 and 4, Study 2 Results, overview and discussion. Live PMC CAPTCHA was not bypassed. Not a full six-study audit.
sources.summary: Reported habits were associated with self-control and selected goal-related outcomes; statistical mediation supported the authors’ proposed account. Study 2 Results associated study habits with lower motivational interference. Mediation is not demonstrated causation. Shared-method variance, reverse paths and residual confounding remain possible. Neither a habit-training intervention nor proof that deliberate inhibition is useless. Do not treat six studies as six independent replications of one identical outcome.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Abstract total N=2,274 across six studies. Verified Methods: Study 1: 500 US MTurk adults (sleep analyses 450); Study 3: 135 undergraduates; Study 4: 447 high-school seniors. Remaining study-specific flow not extracted.
sources.design: Nonrandomized individual-difference/longitudinal observations. Study 1 self-reports assessed trait self-control, frequency/context habits, automaticity and effort; Study 4 added behavioral self-control and later teacher ratings.
sources.population: Selected US adult, undergraduate and high-school samples; study-specific flow remains incompletely extracted.

sources.title: A Stitch in Time: Strategic Self-Control in High School and College Students
sources.accessDepth: Selected search-indexed original Study 2/3 Methods and Results, abstract and limitations. Live PMC CAPTCHA was not bypassed. Study 1 sample 577 is from prior project extraction and was not independently rechecked in this selected pass.
sources.summary: Study 2 modification-versus-combined-controls contrast favored modification (d=.56). Study 3 adjusted pairwise contrasts favored modification (d=.60/.63), controlling baseline study-hours imbalance. Temptation mediation was measured, not randomized. About half of Study 2 lacked follow-up. No statistically significant between-group attrition difference was detected; this does not eliminate attrition bias. Single-item self-report/demand effects, bundled components, short horizon and limited comparator set constrain interpretation. No universal early-strategy superiority or permanent self-control gain.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Study 1: 577 high-school students (descriptive strategy ratings). Study 2: 250 consented, 126 followed up/analyzed (44/35/47 by modification/modulation/control). Study 3: 159 completers (52/52/55); recruited denominator unknown.
sources.design: Random assignment to bundled situation-modification, response-modulation or goal-only activities; videos/endorsements in active arms. Outcomes were one-week self-rated goal accomplishment, not grades or observed goal attainment.
sources.population: High-school and college students; one-week field-experiment self-ratings, with substantial Study 2 attrition.

relatedPublications.title: Retraction: Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment
relatedPublications.note: This 2026 notice retracts the cited Ariely and Wertenbroch (2002) report (DOI 10.1111/1467-9280.00441), not this citing report. Its findings are not inherited as evidence here; this host report and its separately described results are not thereby retracted.

sources.title: Implementation Intentions and Effective Goal Pursuit
sources.accessDepth: Selected live institutional PDF Methods/Results: Study 1 flow, Study 2 pp.191–192, Study 3 pp.193–195. No complete analysis audit.
sources.summary: Study 2 reported timely writing in 12/17 versus 6/19 coded returners (71% versus 32%), not all 86 randomized. No statistically significant difference in overall report-return rates was detected. Study 3 favored timing near a chosen opportunity; overall argument quality did not differ significantly. Study 2 conditions on postrandomization returners and combines planning, visualization and commitment. Narrow tasks and samples; timing/initiation is not universal goal success, permanent habit formation, or metaphysical free will.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Study 1: 111 initial, 92 follow-up, 85 easy-goal and 70 difficult-goal analyses. Study 2: 86 students randomized; 39 returned reports, 36 with usable codes (17 implementation, 19 control). Study 3: 60 male students.
sources.design: Three student studies, including randomized writing-report instructions and a separate action-initiation task; Study 2 result conditions on usable returned reports.
sources.population: Student samples; Study 3 reported 60 male students. Not a broad-population intervention trial.

sources.title: A Multisite Preregistered Paradigmatic Test of the Ego-Depletion Effect
sources.accessDepth: Selected live coauthor-hosted original PDF Methods, exclusion table and confirmatory Table 4; no supplement/raw-data audit.
sources.summary: Confirmatory overall d=.06, 95% CI −.02 to .14; not statistically significant. Exploratory full-sample d=.08 was significant; these are different analyses. No statistically significant trait-belief moderation of the tested effect was detected. Two selected task protocols and substantial exclusions. Does not prove everyday fatigue absent, unrestricted self-command, or that a specific experimentally manipulated belief cannot matter.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 36 laboratories tested 3,531 people; 1,068 preregistered exclusions. Table 4 overall confirmatory endpoint N=2,461, with endpoint-specific missing data.
sources.design: Preregistered multilaboratory project using two selected sequential-task protocols; confirmatory and exploratory analyses are distinct.
sources.population: Participants recruited across 36 laboratories; confirmatory endpoint subset differs from all people tested.

sources.title: A Multilab Replication of the Ego Depletion Effect
sources.accessDepth: Selected live coauthor-institution original PDF Methods, Tables 3/5 and Discussion.
sources.summary: Primary error-rate d=.10, 95% CI .01–.19. After auxiliary exclusions error-rate d remains .10; only reaction-time estimate rises to .16. Willpower-belief moderation appears on secondary reaction time only and was not statistically significant after exclusions. Small protocol-specific effect does not identify resource mechanism. Do not turn abstract d=.16 into an improved primary error-rate result or an unambiguous mindset effect.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 12 laboratories: 1,841 participated, 1,834 completed tasks, 1,775 analyzed after age exclusions; additional sensitivity excludes 340 chance-level performers.
sources.design: Randomized Stroop condition followed by antisaccade task; preregistered primary error-rate analysis, secondary reaction time and auxiliary exclusions.
sources.population: Participants across 12 laboratories; main and auxiliary-exclusion sets differ.

sources.title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect
sources.accessDepth: Selected original report PDF hosted by Columbia: Methods, Table 1, Results/Table 2 and Appendix B. Maastricht mirror returned 403.
sources.summary: Primary reaction-time variability d=.04, 95% CI −.07–.15. Reintroducing accuracy-excluded participants yields primary d=.004, CI −.07–.08, but secondary mean reaction-time d=.08, CI .01–.16. Substantial accuracy exclusions and protocol debates limit generalization. Neither the main null nor a secondary positive endpoint settles all fatigue or a general resource model.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 23 laboratories; 2,141 in reported main analyses, not recruited denominator. Full recruitment total not independently reconciled.
sources.design: Pseudorandomized/block-assigned letter-e task followed by multisource interference task; preregistered exclusions and pooled lab results.
sources.population: Participants across 23 laboratories; full recruitment total remains unreconciled.

sources.title: Ego Depletion—Is It All in Your Head? Implicit Theories About Willpower Affect Self-Regulation
sources.accessDepth: Selected live coauthor original PDF Methods/Results, Study 4 flow and analysis footnotes.
sources.summary: Reported belief-by-depletion interactions in lab tasks and longitudinal associations. Study 3 did not find belief manipulation reduced subjective exhaustion. Small samples, substantial field attrition and later statistical/replication criticism. Measured and manipulated beliefs are different tests. Do not infer fatigue is imaginary, beliefs eliminate physiological limits, or every later null directly replicates Studies 2/3.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Studies 1–3: 60, 46 and 77 students. Study 4: 101 initial, 44 at second wave, 41 in critical final comparison; not one pooled trial.
sources.design: Study 1 measured beliefs; Studies 2/3 used biased-questionnaire belief manipulations; Study 4 observational repeated self-report around exams.
sources.population: Student laboratory samples and a separate repeated self-report exam-period sample.

sources.title: Does willpower mindset really moderate the ego-depletion effect? A preregistered replication of Job, Dweck, and Walton (2010)
sources.accessDepth: Selected live publisher Methods, Results and Limitations; no raw-data or supplement reanalysis.
sources.summary: Did not reproduce depletion main effect or belief moderation in the tested analyses. Planned original logistic model did not converge; authors used alternative fixed/mixed models. Underpowered for small effects; acknowledged preregistration deviations. Tests measured-belief moderation, not a direct replication of experimental belief manipulation. Authors’ concern about original model nesting is not independently established by our review.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 194 randomized (97 per condition); 187 analyzed (95 control, 92 depletion). Age sensitivity N=180.
sources.design: Measured beliefs, randomized letter-cancellation condition; vocal Stroop, added baseline, unblurred text, longer task and altered analysis distinguish it from Job Study 1.
sources.population: Recruited experiment participants; 194 randomized and 187 analyzed, with separate age-sensitivity analysis.

sources.title: How to measure metacognition
sources.accessDepth: Selected live publisher definitions and measurement sections.
sources.summary: Average confidence, discrimination of correct versus incorrect decisions and efficiency relative to task performance are distinct measurements. Metric assumptions matter; one confidence rating cannot establish all dimensions, and ratios can become unstable at low sensitivity. This is a measurement account, not a training trial.
sources.sampleSizeNote: No new participant sample: conceptual/statistical methods review.
sources.design: Conceptual and statistical methods review.
sources.population: Not applicable: no newly recruited sample.

sources.title: Domain-General Enhancements of Metacognitive Ability Through Adaptive Training
sources.accessDepth: Selected live original PMC Methods/Results/Discussion; no raw-data reanalysis.
sources.summary: Composite calibration improved and transferred to an untrained recognition-memory task. Evidence for cross-domain transfer of the separate efficiency and confidence components was equivocal. Attrition, narrow tasks and the later shared-data critique limit a general training conclusion.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 102 completed the first session; 8 floor/ceiling exclusions, 25 dropouts, 1 technical and 7 quality exclusions; 61 analyzed (29 experimental, 32 control).
sources.design: Randomized feedback-by-stimulus groups; eight perceptual-training sessions plus pre/post tests, with an active accuracy-feedback control.
sources.population: Participants in narrow perceptual-training and recognition-memory tasks; substantial attrition and exclusions.

sources.title: Metacognitive Improvement: Disentangling Adaptive Training From Experimental Confounds
sources.accessDepth: Selected live original coauthor-hosted PDF Methods/Results/Discussion.
sources.summary: A reanalysis and changed-protocol new arm questioned the original training interpretation. The group-by-time efficiency interaction was nonsignificant, with BF=.17 favoring the null under the selected model. The new arm reused the original control group; it was not an independent randomized two-arm replication or proof that all training fails.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 69 started; 18 analyzed after 11 dropout, 9 screening, 19 technical, 11 floor/ceiling and 1 confidence-variance exclusions. Original 32-person control reused, not newly recruited.
sources.design: Preregistered sequential design with a new experimental arm only; rewards throughout, a consistent scale, original-data reanalysis and reused original control.
sources.population: Selected new training-arm participants plus the original Carpenter control; not independent participant sets.

sources.title: The Impact of Feedback on Perceptual Decision-Making and Metacognition: Reduction in Bias but No Change in Sensitivity
sources.accessDepth: Selected live publisher Methods/Results and measurement definitions.
sources.summary: Experiment 1 Task 1 showed reduced response bias and a stronger across-person confidence–performance association. Calibration/criterion transfer to the unreinforced Task 2 was not statistically significant. Feedback-related sensitivity improvements were not statistically significant across both experiments; Experiment 2 was sensitivity-focused and underpowered for bias.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Experiment 1: 443; task-specific exclusions of 48/47 leave 395/396. Experiment 2: 75 seven-day completers, 60 analyzed; initial recruitment denominator not extracted.
sources.design: MTurk adults randomized to feedback/no-feedback. Experiment 1 Task 1 received the manipulation; Task 2 received no feedback in either group. Experiment 2 tested seven-day sensitivity effects.
sources.population: MTurk adult convenience samples; task-specific and seven-day follow-up analysis sets.

sources.title: Confidence ratings do not distinguish imagination from reality
sources.accessDepth: Selected indexed original Methods/Results/Discussion; live PMC CAPTCHA and publisher PDF 403 stopped.
sources.summary: Modeled local confidence criteria followed imagery-related presence-response shifts, while post-task reports showed some global insight. This does not imply total absence of self-knowledge or uniquely identify a perceptual mechanism. Selected Experiment 2 subset/statistic labels remain unresolved and are not silently corrected.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Experiment 1: 130 completed, 102 analyzed; 51 answered the global-insight question. Experiment 2: 130 completed, 111 analyzed and 111 structured global-insight responses. Other endpoint subsets differ.
sources.design: Imagery versus no-imagery gratings during near-threshold detection with modeled confidence criteria. Preregistered plan changed after initial data; two Experiment 1 batches were pooled.
sources.population: Online near-threshold grating-detection participants; local confidence and post-task question denominators differ.

sources.title: Confidence reports during perceptual decision making dissociate from changes in subjective experience
sources.accessDepth: Selected final published institutional PDF Methods, Experiment 1/2 Results, Figures 2/3/5 captions and Limitations; not a complete article/supplement audit.
sources.summary: Confidence shifted under all three manipulations in both experiments. Combined reproduction data distinguished the illusion from base-rate/payoff effects; confidence alone did not uniquely diagnose perceptual change. Restricted manipulations and reproduction benchmark assumptions constrain inference. Experiment 2 alone provided inconclusive evidence for no reproduction effect of the base-rate/payoff manipulations; combined evidence was stronger. No raw-data/supplement audit or direct imagery replication; the recruited-to-analyzed flow remains partly unreconciled.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 122 and 123 participated in Experiments 1/2; figure captions report 108 and 96 analyzed (combined 204). Experiment 2 exclusion-category counts do not reconcile by simple subtraction; overlap or reporting explanation remains unresolved.
sources.design: Nonpreregistered line-length tasks comparing three between-person bias manipulations (Müller–Lyer, base rate, asymmetric payoff), with within-person bias direction and controlled reproduction. Confidence was concurrent in Experiment 1 and postdecision in Experiment 2; Bayesian sequential stopping in Experiment 1.
sources.population: Participants in line-length experiments; 122 and 123 participated, with 108 and 96 analyzed according to figure captions. Experiment 2 exclusion-category arithmetic remains unresolved.

sources.title: Predicting adolescent cognitive and self-regulatory competencies from preschool delay of gratification: Identifying diagnostic conditions
sources.accessDepth: Selected original author-lab PDF Methods, Tables 1/4, SAT Results and Discussion, printed pp.979–985; not all item-level analyses audited.
sources.summary: Preschool waiting was associated with selected adolescent outcomes most strongly under exposed-reward/no-suggested-strategy conditions. The focal SAT subgroup of 35 had reported verbal r=.42 and quantitative r=.57. Selective follow-up, condition-specific subsets and parent reports limit generalization; task-condition randomization does not make observed waiting time a randomized long-term intervention.
sources.design: Longitudinal observational follow-up of preschool laboratory participants. Original task conditions varied, but individual waiting time was not randomized as a training intervention.
sources.population: University-community preschool sample followed into adolescence; 185 returned at least one assessment, with smaller outcome- and condition-specific subsets.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 653 original participants; 550 standard-task eligible; 404 presumed deliverable follow-up invitations; 185 returned at least one assessment. Parent-reported SAT was available for 94; the exposed-reward/no-suggested-strategy SAT subgroup had 35.

sources.title: Revisiting the Marshmallow Test: A Conceptual Replication Investigating Links Between Early Delay of Gratification and Later Outcomes
sources.accessDepth: Original journal PDF on public mirror; selected Methods pp.2–7, Results p.9/Table 4 and limitations/open practices pp.17–18. Publisher abstract and PMC indexed metadata corroborated; no complete supplemental audit.
sources.summary: In the focal maternal-no-college subgroup, the standardized age-15 achievement association was .24 unadjusted, .08 with earlier/background controls and .05 with concurrent controls (p=.140 for the last). Behavioral-composite associations were not statistically significant. Adjustment changes the conditional question; this observational, nonpreregistered conceptual replication neither isolates a causal mechanism nor proves that waiting interventions cannot help. The Watts, Michaelson and Sperber reports reuse the NICHD SECCYD cohort with different subsets, outcomes and analyses. Participant-level intersections were not independently reconstructed. They are not three independent replications; do not sum their sample sizes.
sources.design: Nonpreregistered longitudinal secondary analysis with unadjusted and successively adjusted models; conceptual, not exact, replication of the Stanford follow-up.
sources.population: Ten-site NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development cohort, followed to age 15; not nationally representative, with a seven-minute preschool-task ceiling.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 918 analyzed: 552 in the maternal-no-college subgroup and 366 in the maternal-college subgroup. These are subgroups of one cohort, not separate recruited studies.

sources.title: Same Data Set, Different Conclusions: Preschool Delay of Gratification Predicts Later Behavioral Outcomes in a Preregistered Study
sources.accessDepth: PubMed abstract, indexed original first page and indexed primary Discussion/limitations read. Live PMC CAPTCHA and institutional PDF rate limit prevented full Methods/Results inspection.
sources.summary: Reports associations for three of five outcomes and problem-behavior associations across models. Its Discussion identifies different behavioral measures, repeated-observation models, whole-sample use and theory-led controls compared with Watts. This is another analysis of the same cohort, not independent replication. Detailed Methods, estimates and analysis-specific sample sizes were not fully inspected; the proposed social-support account is observational, not experimentally established mediation. The Watts, Michaelson and Sperber reports reuse the NICHD SECCYD cohort with different subsets, outcomes and analyses. Participant-level intersections were not independently reconstructed. They are not three independent replications; do not sum their sample sizes.
sources.design: Preregistered longitudinal secondary analysis of the SECCYD cohort using differing outcomes and models; detailed Methods/Results not fully inspected.
sources.population: NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development cohort reused; exact analysis-specific denominator not extracted. Do not substitute the sample size from another report.

sources.title: Delay of gratification and adult outcomes: The Marshmallow Test does not reliably predict adult functioning
sources.accessDepth: Selected original journal PDF Methods, Results/Tables 2–4 and limitations, with publisher/PubMed abstract corroboration. Not complete supplemental or raw-data audit.
sources.summary: Fully adjusted continuous-delay analyses did not detect statistically significant associations across nine age-26 outcomes. An exploratory, nonpreregistered full-seven-minute indicator retained a BMI association without multiplicity adjustment. Other categorical specifications yielded different patterns; these two summaries do not describe every specification. Nondetection is not equivalence. Attrition, the seven-minute ceiling, adjustment choices and unresolved Table 1 denominators limit interpretation. The Watts, Michaelson and Sperber reports reuse the NICHD SECCYD cohort with different subsets, outcomes and analyses. Participant-level intersections were not independently reconstructed. They are not three independent replications; do not sum their sample sizes.
sources.design: Preregistered longitudinal secondary analysis with continuous-delay models; the separate full-seven-minute indicator analysis was exploratory and nonpreregistered. No randomized waiting-training intervention.
sources.population: NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development cohort followed to age 26; adult analysis n=702, 83% White and 46% male, with endpoint-specific availability and attrition.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Original cohort 1,364; 1,038 administered the task; 72 invalid records and 5 without a time left 961 valid task records. Adult analysis included 702 with a valid preschool task and at least one age-26 outcome; not 702 observations for every endpoint.

sources.title: Putting brain training to the test
sources.design: Six-week randomized online training comparison: reasoning/planning tasks or mixed cognitive tasks versus active online knowledge questions. Analysis retained participants with both benchmark assessments, despite the article’s intention-to-treat label.
sources.population: BBC-viewer volunteers aged 18–60; general cognitive training, not targeted clinical rehabilitation.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 52,617 registered; 11,430 were included in the reported baseline/six-week analysis: 4,678 reasoning/planning, 4,014 mixed training and 2,738 control. These are retained analysis groups, not initial randomized denominators; control dropout was greater.
sources.accessDepth: Author-hosted publisher PDF, all five main-article pages including online Methods; Tables 1–3 and discussion inspected, Table 2 visually checked. Supplementary inventory/captions only; no full supplement or raw-data audit.
sources.summary: Practiced-task scores improved. Untrained reasoning-change differences versus active control were small and positive (d=.17 and .22; 99% CIs .10–.23 and .15–.28); other memory results differed by endpoint and sometimes favored control. This is not universal nondetection or demonstrated broad everyday benefit. Six-week testing was at the end of training, not delayed retention. The 2016 synthesis listed here excluded this report because its required far-transfer outcomes differed.

sources.title: Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory
sources.design: Four matched training/no-training cohorts using adaptive dual n-back practice for 8, 12, 17 or 19 sessions. Original Methods do not report participant randomization or an active control.
sources.population: Healthy young adults recruited from the University of Bern community; mean age 25.6 years.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 70 initially: 35 training and 35 control. One training participant failed to complete required sessions, leaving 34 training and 35 control analyzed. Cohort totals are not additional participants.
sources.accessDepth: Original author-hosted publisher PDF Methods, Results and Discussion inspected; Figure 3 visually checked. No raw-data audit or independent reconstruction of later unpublished additions.
sources.summary: A positive training-by-session interaction was reported on speeded matrix tests (partial η²=.07), with posttesting 1–2 days after training. This is not a standardized IQ-point increase. Matrix test choice differed by cohort; longer-cohort gains are not randomized dose evidence. The later synthesis includes this study family plus author-supplied active-control data and working-memory outcomes absent from the original article; those additions do not change the original passive-control design.

sources.title: No Evidence of Intelligence Improvement After Working Memory Training: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study
sources.design: Dual n-back versus visual-search active control and no-contact control, with 20 training sessions. Initial matching and dropout replacements were followed by a later wave randomized only between training arms; not simple random allocation of the full three-arm sample.
sources.population: Adults aged 18–30, mostly university students at two US sites; not a clinical rehabilitation sample.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 130 at least pretested; 75 completed; two control completers excluded for repeated test items, leaving 73 cognitive-analysis participants: 24 n-back, 29 visual-search and 20 control. Some cognitive endpoints have smaller denominators; the daily-activity survey uses a partly different set.
sources.accessDepth: Coauthor-hosted publisher PDF Methods, Results, Tables 1–5 and selected discussion/limitations inspected; selected tables visually checked. Official supplement tables and captions read; no raw-data audit.
sources.summary: Both training groups improved on practiced tasks. No statistically significant positive cognitive transfer was detected at the article-stated α=.01 threshold; this does not exclude small effects. Some n-back participants reported daily-activity changes, but actual behavior was not verified. No delayed retention test was reported. This report is included in the 2016 synthesis and is not an additional independent confirmation of that synthesis; 2012 online-first and 2013 issue publication are one report.

sources.title: Working Memory Training Does Not Improve Performance on Measures of Intelligence or Other Measures of “Far Transfer”: Evidence From a Meta-Analytic Review
sources.design: Random-effects meta-analysis of computerized working-memory training with treated or untreated controls; report-defined criterion, related working-memory and far-transfer outcomes analyzed separately.
sources.population: Unselected samples and samples with cognitive or learning difficulties. Overall estimates are not healthy-only or a targeted rehabilitation efficacy estimate.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 87 publications and 145 reported comparisons, with overlapping groups and outcome-specific counts; these are not 145 independently verified samples. No unique participant total is inferred or pooled here.
sources.accessDepth: Published-format UCL PDF selected Methods, Results, discussion and Tables 1–2 inspected, with main tables visually checked. Publisher supplement selectively parsed; complete binary, supplementary visual audit and workbook unavailable.
sources.summary: Treated-control estimates favored criterion/related working-memory tasks; the overall nonverbal-ability estimate was g=.05 (95% CI −.02 to .13). Positive reading-comprehension, delayed-arithmetic and selected subgroup estimates must remain distinct from author sensitivity analyses; not every estimate was null. Follow-up was sparse and varied, averaging about five months. The synthesis includes Jaeggi and Redick study families but excludes Owen. Review and included reports are not independent confirmations; supplementary Jaeggi data exceed the published original article.

sources.title: Grateful recounting enhances subjective well-being: The importance of grateful processing
sources.design: Reported random assignment to one week of gratitude recounting, comparative-pride processing or semantic-memory writing. Analysis selected completers who met adherence criteria; random sequence/concealment and the initial randomized denominator were not established from the inspected report.
sources.population: Nonclinical undergraduate psychology-course participants; exact age range unreported in inspected Methods. Do not assume every participant was an adult.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 129 included completers/adherers: 47 gratitude, 42 comparative pride and 40 semantic memory. Inclusion required outcome assessments and at least four of seven activities. Initial recruitment/randomization totals and arm-specific attrition remain unknown.
sources.accessDepth: Selected original Methods, Results, Table 1 and Discussion read through an author-posted article text. Publisher direct access failed; no local PDF/table-image verification or raw-data reanalysis.
sources.summary: Baseline-adjusted composite wellbeing favored gratitude across post-activity assessments against the two specified writing controls. The time-by-condition interaction was not statistically significant; separate occasion analyses found a statistically significant overall condition effect only at five weeks; the immediate and one-week tests were not statistically significant. This does not demonstrate continuing differential improvement. Follow-ups belong to one experiment, not separate replications. The report was not found in the inspected included-study tables/references of the listed 2016 synthesis; participant-level independence was not verified.

sources.title: Thankful for the Little Things: A Meta-Analysis of Gratitude Interventions
sources.design: Historical random-effects synthesis of reported randomized gratitude interventions, with measurement-only, activity-matched and psychologically active comparison categories. Search dated March 2014; not an updated comprehensive review.
sources.population: Mixed ages, samples and gratitude formats, predominantly college students but also school-age, community and older groups. Not an adult-writing-only estimate.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 26 manuscripts and 32 reported samples. The wellbeing contrasts include activity-matched k=18, n=1,391 and psychologically active k=9, n=1,012. These overlap with broader comparisons and other outcomes; do not sum them into unique participants or independent confirmations.
sources.accessDepth: Selected original publisher-format text Methods, Results/Table 1, included-study tables, Discussion and relevant references inspected. No local visual verification of Table 1, supplemental Appendix read or raw-data reanalysis.
sources.summary: Reported wellbeing differences were small versus activity-matched tasks (d=.14, 95% CI .01 to .27), while the psychologically active comparison was not statistically distinguishable from zero (d=−.03, −.13 to .07). The former no longer excluded zero under the authors’ trim-and-fill sensitivity; that method is not a corrected true effect. Overlapping contrasts are not independent replications. Watkins 2008 appears in the synthesis, but the listed Watkins 2015 report was not found in inspected inclusion material; this does not certify participant-level independence. No separate long-term persistence estimate was established here.

sources.title: Does a Favor Request Increase Liking Toward the Requester?
sources.design: Random-lot assignment to a confederate’s friendly personal request or an experimenter’s instruction to help that same confederate in a low-cost puzzle task; baseline and immediate post-task ratings in two country samples. Both groups helped.
sources.population: Undergraduates in Japan (41; ages 18–27; 76% women) and the US (42; ages 18–21; 74% women; 95% White or Caucasian). Confederates were women from the corresponding social group.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 83 reported participants: Japan, 22 personal-request and 19 experimenter-instruction; US, 22 and 20. These cells total 83. A separate earlier recruitment/screening denominator and exclusion flow were not established; do not interpret 83 as a verified initial-recruitment count.
sources.accessDepth: Selected original accepted-manuscript Methods, Results, Table 1, footnotes and Discussion read through web-extracted text. Publisher/direct binary access failed; no local PDF-byte or visual table verification, complete-document read or raw-data reanalysis.
sources.summary: Immediate liking change was greater after the confederate’s friendly personal-request package than experimenter-instructed help. The measures concern liking, friendship interest, social impression and closeness, not romantic desire or durable attachment. Requester identity/authority and wording changed together; an affiliative mechanism was not independently isolated. Online 2015 and issue 2016 are one report; two country samples and multiple outcomes are not independent report votes.

sources.title: If You Need Help, Just Ask: Underestimating Compliance With Direct Requests for Help
sources.design: Selected Study 5 used hypothetical helper/requester perspectives and direct/indirect request scenarios, with a separate anticipated-discomfort check. Selected Study 6 compared direct verbal requests with silently distributed flyers and two questionnaire lengths. Study 5 role randomization is explicit; random allocation for its directness factor and Study 6 was not established in the inspected wording.
sources.population: Study 5: Columbia students and financial-services employees. Study 6: Columbia students requesting help from strangers. These selected studies are not a population estimate or a study of romantic relationships.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Selected Study 5 reports 83 completers: 57 students and 26 employees; its separate manipulation-check sample size is not established. Study 6 reports 99 initially, 16 withdrawals and 4 incomplete cases, leaving 79 analyzed completers. Exact four-cell allocation remains unreconciled. No report-wide pooled participant total is asserted.
sources.accessDepth: Selected original Studies 5–6 Methods, Results and adjacent Discussion read in a mirrored Cornell-cover electronic reprint, with institutional identity metadata checked. Earlier-study summary passages were inspected for context, not all six studies adjudicated. The mirror was not byte-certified against a downloaded Cornell original; no raw-data reanalysis.
sources.summary: The inspected evidence concerns anticipated refusal discomfort, expected compliance and task responses—not liking or romantic attraction. Study 5 judgments are hypothetical; actual field recipients’ motives were not established by them. Study 6 bundles request mode with contact and return logistics and uses a capped flyer-response proxy. The original coauthor name is Vanessa K. B. Lake, later indexed as Vanessa K. Bohns; this is one report, not two. Its selected studies are not confirmations of Niiya’s liking finding.

sources.title: Ask me why, don’t tell me why: Asking children for explanations facilitates relational thinking
sources.design: Randomized child geometric-card task: 23 per arm received identical adult demonstrations. Twelve same-relation triads comprised six adult demonstrations and six child choices, alternating in two-trial blocks. After adult and own choices, the explain group was asked why and the report group which card was chosen. No corrective feedback; reporting was an active choice-report comparison, not a supplied explanation or passive rest.
sources.population: Museum-recruited children aged 58.6–82.9 months. No adult comparison group.
sources.sampleSizeNote: One report and one included sample of 46 children, randomized 23 per arm; six additional children were excluded (five experimenter error, one incomplete). Published article and author manuscript are versions of this same report, not independent confirmations.
sources.accessDepth: Selected Methods, Results and Discussion in the published author-lab PDF, sections 2–4 (pages 3–8), inspected; pages 4–5 also visually inspected. Author manuscript inspected online as another version of the same report. Not a complete-document or systematic field review; no raw-data/code reanalysis or independent retraction check.
sources.summary: The explain group made more task-correct choices across six immediate new-shape trials than the report group (means 4.78 versus 1.44; reported between-arm mean-difference 95% CI 2.08–4.61 out of six). This is immediate within-task new-item generalization, not a separate transfer test or delayed retention. Because every target relation was same, choosing the identical-pair card without comparing its relation with the target could succeed. Prompts followed both adult and own choices, so the bundle does not isolate explaining adult examples alone. Representation change is an interpretation, not an experimentally established mediator. No adult comparison, IQ outcome or AI condition was tested. Online 2022 and issue 2023 identify one report/sample; no universal learning or adult-intelligence claim follows.

sources.title: Asking People to Explain Complex Policies Does Not Increase Political Moderation: Three Preregistered Failures to Closely Replicate Fernbach, Rogers, Fox, and Sloman’s (2013) Findings
sources.design: Three preregistered US MTurk experiments; randomized mechanistic-explanation versus reasons conditions. Two tested immediate pre/post self-rated understanding and policy-position extremity; a third tested a small donation choice and added group-bias measures.
sources.population: US online convenience samples; not recruited as extremists.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Recruited 306/405/343; attention-passing 302/377/341 (total 1020), with outcome-level missingness. Samples were nonoverlapping within this project; three experiments in one report, not three independent research teams. Only the first two samples (679 attention-passing, before outcome missingness) assess understanding/extremity; 1020 is not a pooled outcome denominator.
sources.accessDepth: Author-hosted published full report methods/results/discussion inspected (pp 612–620). Preregistration/data links recorded but not independently audited or reanalyzed. No exhaustive review or retraction audit.
sources.summary: Mechanistic explanations lowered self-rated understanding in two close replications, but neither reproduced reduced position extremity. The third did not reproduce the original donation interaction. These immediate outcomes do not establish objective calibration or durable depolarization. Changed attention checks and incompletely available original materials qualify replication fidelity; nonsignificance is not proof of universal absence.

sources.title: The Effect of Mood-Context on Visual Recognition and Recall Memory
sources.design: Randomized four-cell film-induced neutral/stressful encoding and retrieval experiment; 15 participants per cell. Symbol recall and face recognition followed a 20-minute filler and retrieval induction.
sources.population: Adult undergraduates; laboratory visual-memory tasks, not classroom learning.
sources.sampleSizeNote: One 60-person sample. Recall and recognition are outcomes from this sample, not independent replications.
sources.accessDepth: Institutional accepted manuscript Methods, Results, Discussion and figures inspected, with independent AI critique. No raw-data reanalysis, exhaustive review or retraction audit.
sources.summary: A matching interaction coexisted with better performance after neutral encoding. No simple-effect post-hoc contrasts were reported; plotted stressed-retrieval scores appear similar across encoding conditions, a descriptive observation rather than an equivalence test. The interaction alone does not show that stressful study improves later stressed performance. Small cells, short delay and film/mood-context confounding limit inference. Inconsistent printed main-effect eta values are not used here. No exam, durable-transfer or custom-method benefit was tested.

sources.title: Learning under stress impairs memory formation
sources.design: Randomized socially evaluated cold-water stress versus warm-water control; word learning started ten seconds after stressor onset, with recall and recognition tested 24 hours later.
sources.population: Healthy university volunteers aged 19–39; 16 men and 32 women.
sources.sampleSizeNote: One 48-person sample, with two delayed-memory outcomes; not two independent confirmations.
sources.accessDepth: Author-university published article Methods and Results, pages 184–186 and Figures 2–3, inspected with independent AI critique. No raw-data reanalysis or retraction audit.
sources.summary: Stressed learners recalled fewer words (5.0 versus 7.3) and had lower recognition sensitivity (d-prime 1.13 versus 1.67) at 24 hours. Retrieval stress was not varied. Pain, distraction and social evaluation were bundled; no unique cortisol mechanism was isolated. Without an immediate learning test, acquisition cannot be separated from consolidation. This result does not generalize to all arousal, useful challenge or contextual rehearsal. Educational transfer was not tested.

sources.title: The impact of threat of shock-induced anxiety on the neural substrates of memory encoding and retrieval
sources.design: Counterbalanced within-person safe/threat-of-shock encoding and retrieval conditions during face-recognition and spatial-memory fMRI tasks, separated by seconds.
sources.population: Healthy adults; psychiatric history and general ill health excluded.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Main task samples were 32 for face recognition and 33 for spatial memory; overlapping participants, not 65 independent cases. A separate 20-person pilot is not included in this denominator.
sources.accessDepth: Public publisher Methods, Behavioral Results and Discussion inspected with independent AI critique. No participant-data reanalysis, exhaustive review or retraction audit.
sources.summary: Threat at face encoding reduced accuracy. The spatial behavioral matching advantage reported by Bolton and Robinson (2017), not Robinson and Rollings’s mood-context report, did not replicate in the modified scanner task. A hippocampal matching contrast pooled across both tasks occurred without corresponding behavioral improvement. Changed controls and time limits qualify replication fidelity; nonsignificance does not prove no effect. Neither delayed retention nor educational transfer was tested.

sources.title: Goal Striving, Need Satisfaction, and Longitudinal Well-Being: The Self-Concordance Model
sources.design: Three longitudinal student cohorts with self-rated goal reasons, effort, attainment, need satisfaction and wellbeing; no randomized goal selection.
sources.population: University students followed across a semester.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Reported samples: 169, 152 and 73. Study 3 includes people completing at least six of eight questionnaires; its starting enrollment and attrition denominator were not established. Studies 1 and 2 reuse previously reported datasets; do not count those reports again as independent samples.
sources.accessDepth: Selected Methods, Results and limitations in the original report, pages 485–486, 488–492 and 494–495, read using OCR with independent AI critique. This is not a systematic review, raw-data replication or comprehensive retraction audit.
sources.summary: Self-concordance was prospectively associated with self-reported effort and progress. Covariate adjustment in Study 3 does not randomize goal choice or eliminate all confounding. Study 2 examines need satisfaction and wellbeing, not an intervention assigning personally authentic goals. These associations do not establish an objective completion advantage or efficacy of the authored method. This report and the classroom-framing report share an author and theoretical lineage, not three wholly independent research traditions.

sources.title: Attaining Personal Goals: Self-Concordance Plus Implementation Intentions Equals Success
sources.design: Study 1 randomized a when/where plus distraction-counterstrategy planning package versus no prompted planning. Study 2 randomized reflection on meaningful reasons and rewarding process aspects of existing resolutions, planning, or no-prompt control.
sources.population: McGill undergraduates pursuing weekend goals; a separate New Year’s-resolution sample.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Study 1: 106. Study 2: 61 recruited, two initial-only participants excluded, 59 in principal analyses; three-month responses from 36 of 61. Different samples, horizons and progress scales are not a pooled success rate.
sources.accessDepth: Original report Methods and Results, pages 234–240, inspected with independent AI critique; page 239 statistics visually checked. No raw-data, allocation-sequence or author-correction verification; no comprehensive retraction audit.
sources.summary: Study 1 reported 68% versus 55% self-rated weekend progress, not percentages of people with verified completion; the package also requested three distractions and three counterstrategies, so when/where planning was not isolated. In Study 2, the authors reported higher self-concordance ratings after reflection in a planned contrast; neither intervention demonstrated a one-month progress benefit. Self-concordance was assessed two weeks after assignment, not randomized goal authenticity or a clean baseline moderator. Baseline goal difficulty was imbalanced. Three-month intervention effects and the interaction pattern were nonsignificant, with substantial loss to follow-up; nulls do not prove equivalence. The one-month affect/progress association was marginal, not a demonstrated wellbeing benefit. Reporting inconsistencies remain unresolved: Methods calls progress 9-point, Results 7-point; the printed omnibus F(1,55)=3.53 with p<.05 is numerically inconsistent (nominal tail about .066), while planned-contrast F(1,54)=4.77 is compatible with p<.05. The omnibus degrees of freedom are also unclear for three groups; regression text/table degrees of freedom and interaction t values differ. These are reader consistency checks, not author-corrected results. Embedded meta-analyses are not independent replications.

sources.title: Motivating Learning, Performance, and Persistence: The Synergistic Effects of Intrinsic Goal Contents and Autonomy-Supportive Contexts
sources.design: Three within-class randomized experiments crossed intrinsic versus extrinsic written framing with autonomy-supportive versus controlling wording; no neutral arm. Instructors were blind to assignment.
sources.population: Belgian high-school and college students completing recycling, communication or Tai-bo activities.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Separate reported study samples of 200, 377 and 224; multiple outcomes within each sample are not independent replications.
sources.accessDepth: Original report Methods, Results and Discussion, especially pages 248–256, inspected with independent AI critique. Page 256 inconsistency visually confirmed; additional interaction flags from extracted text only. No raw-data, preregistration, author-erratum or comprehensive retraction verification.
sources.summary: Reported short-term performance and voluntary-participation main effects favored intrinsic framing and autonomy-supportive wording. Library entry does not establish reading, and demonstration volunteering does not establish sustained completion. Without a neutral arm, contrasts cannot separate benefits over neutral instruction from harms of controlling or extrinsic framing. Persistence interactions were not conventionally significant; a combined-condition contrast is not evidence of interaction or synergy. Measured motivational mediation was not independently randomized. These experiments assigned framing, not free selection of life goals. The printed page 256 performance-interaction F(1,220)=4.10 with p<.001 is inconsistent (nominal tail about .044); extracted-text performance-interaction pairs on pages 250 and 254 also warrant checking. These are reader audit flags, not author corrections or evidence of fabrication, and fragile interaction thresholds are not used here.

sources.title: I understand you feel that way, but I feel this way: the benefits of I-language and communicating perspective during conflict
sources.design: Within-person vignette-rating study crossing I/you language with four perspective conditions; six hypothetical scenarios and eight opening statements per scenario, presented in random order.
sources.population: University students judging hypothetical romantic-partner, friend and colleague disagreements.
sources.sampleSizeNote: 253 university students; mean age 28, SD 8.75; 77% women. All participants rated the variants: these are not eight independent participant groups.
sources.accessDepth: Preserved PMC full-report HTML methods, results, Table 1 and limitations inspected with independent AI critique. The failed publisher download was HTML, not a scientific PDF. Supplement, participant data and recruitment/exclusion flow beyond the analytic sample were not independently audited; no comprehensive integrity or retraction audit.
sources.summary: The report found lower predicted-defensiveness ratings for I-language than its you-language versions, and lower ratings when both perspectives were communicated than in the other perspective conditions. Actual defensive behavior was not measured. Wording changed more than pronouns alone, including expressing understanding or presenting a request as the speaker’s thought. Participants saw all alternatives and knew both protagonists’ perspectives, allowing comparative judgment and demand effects. No isolated always/never-versus-specific-behavior comparison, actual dyadic conflict, comprehension or durable relationship outcome was tested. This is adjacent wording context, not support for expressive-suppression effects.

sources.title: Conversational receptiveness: Improving engagement with opposing views
sources.design: Selected Study 4 randomized writers to a four-strategy receptiveness package plus receptive-language instruction or unrelated fish reading plus natural response; separate opposing-view readers rated the texts. Studies 2–3 provide observational context, not randomized language comparisons.
sources.population: MTurk writers and ideologically opposed raters evaluating written disagreement about campus sexual assault and police relations.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Study 4: 771 final writers and 1,548 raters; each rater evaluated two disagreeing writers, with about four ratings per text. These are distinct roles, not 2,319 independent experimental writers. Post-treatment attrition was 17.2% versus 12.6%; eligible attention/check-passing completers were retained.
sources.accessDepth: Full published author-hosted PDF, selected Studies 2–4 methods/results and intervention appendix, inspected with independent AI critique. Materials, preregistrations and raw data were not independently audited; no comprehensive integrity or retraction audit.
sources.summary: Study 4 reported improved immediate receptiveness and collaboration-intention ratings by opposing-view readers after a package teaching positive framing, acknowledging understanding, points of agreement and hedging, with comprehension checks and instructions to use receptive language. The comparator was unrelated reading and natural response. Post-treatment selection limits the causal package interpretation. These are reader evaluations and intentions, not demonstrated comprehension, observed collaboration, attitude change or experimentally prevented escalation. The experiment does not isolate any strategy, pronoun, behavior-specific description or custom script. No sustained adoption was measured. Government-manager dyads and Wikipedia threads elsewhere in this report are observational; their language associations do not establish prevention or assign responsibility to attacked people. This single report’s studies, outcomes and publication versions are not independent report votes; later reuse of its data is not independent replication.

sources.title: Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth
sources.design: Two principal reported experiments; counterbalanced repeated/new statements after initial interest ratings. Six-point truth ratings in E1 and binary judgments in E2.
sources.population: Duke undergraduates.
sources.sampleSizeNote: Two principal reported samples, n=40 each; participant identity overlap unknown. A briefly described further n=16 experiment is not independently audited support or an additional adjudicated sample.
sources.accessDepth: Original journal PDF: https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/fazio-jepgen2015.pdf — journal pp.994–997 methods/results; pp.998–1000 models/discussion. Original methods/results inspected with independent AI critique; no raw-data reanalysis or comprehensive retraction audit.
sources.summary: Two principal reported Duke-undergraduate samples, n=40 each. A further n=16 experiment is briefly described on journal p.996 without detailed methods; it is not independently audited support or an additional adjudicated sample in this review. Exposure: interest ratings for 88 statements; immediate test: 176 repeated/new statements, counterbalanced. Participants were warned about true/false items. E1 used a six-point truth scale and subsequent knowledge check; falsehood analyses: repeated 3.53 versus new 3.26, F(1,39)=13.06, p=.001. Demonstrated-known falsehoods: 2.93 versus 2.59; unknown: 4.13 versus 3.92. E2 used binary judgments, norm-estimated knowledge, no individual knowledge check: repeated .62 versus new .56 across truth statuses, not a falsehood-only acceptance rate. E1’s retrospective knowledge classification can be affected by exposure; E2’s norms are not individual knowledge. Small, selected samples and narrow trivia restrict transfer. Fluency-conditional modeling outperformed the tested alternative; this does not experimentally identify a unique psychological mechanism. No participant-overlap declaration was located; treat as two reported samples, not verified identity-disjoint samples. Shared authors/lab with Brashier et al. (2020) reduce investigative independence.

disciplines.title: Legitimate Authority
disciplines.learningGoal: Scope, competence, and right to act.
disciplines.practice: Choose an ordinary shared decision. List what you control, what you can influence, and what belongs to another person. Ask where consent or expertise changes your authority.

disciplines.title: Awareness
disciplines.practice: Record one ordinary event in five columns: observed event, bodily sensation, interpretation, urge, chosen action. Mark every inference explicitly.
disciplines.artifact: Five correctly distinguished facts and inferences with a revised entry.

disciplines.title: Understanding
disciplines.practice: Choose two explanations for one event. For each, state what you would expect to see and what would count against it. Leave unknowns visible.
disciplines.artifact: A mechanism map with rival predictions and a discriminating observation.

disciplines.title: Discernment
disciplines.practice: Find a claim you care about. Seek the strongest relevant counterevidence. Write what changed, what did not, and how your conduct will differ.
disciplines.artifact: One warranted belief revision tied to a specific change in action.

disciplines.title: Integration
disciplines.practice: Plan an ordinary conversation that calls for both firmness and care. Define one action for each, then reflect on whether both were expressed.
disciplines.artifact: A two-capacity practice record, including tensions and limits.

disciplines.title: Self-Command
disciplines.practice: Pick a manageable, low-stakes task. Choose observable conduct while allowing ordinary feelings to remain. Test it across contexts without escalating distress.

disciplines.title: Competence
disciplines.practice: Define a useful task, its performance criterion and a new context. Test it, retain failures, and teach back what the evidence supports.
disciplines.artifact: Observable performance, an acknowledged failure, and a teaching artifact.

disciplines.title: Stewardship
disciplines.practice: Plan how to notice drift, recover after a setback, and update your model. Export a record and choose your own later review date.
